sentences.text: Now the differences in vessels and lights.
There are eight, and you’ve met every one of them already.
Constrained by draft exists only in the International rules: three red lights, or a cylinder.
Inland, there’s no such vessel.
A vessel pushing ahead, seen from astern.
International: a sternlight.
Inland: two yellow towing lights.
The barge she pushes.
International: sidelights.
Inland: sidelights plus a special flashing yellow light.
On the Great Lakes, a power-driven vessel may carry an all-round white light in place of the after masthead light and sternlight.
Rivers.
On the Great Lakes and Western Rivers, the downbound vessel with a following current has the right of way, and a vessel crossing the river keeps clear.
The International rules have nothing like it.
A vessel under twenty meters in a special anchorage area.
Inland, she needs no anchor light or signal.
The motorsailing cone on a vessel under twelve meters.
International: required.
Inland: optional.
And distress.
Inland adds the white light flashing fifty to seventy times a minute.
Notice the theme.
Nearly every Inland difference is about rivers, towboats, or small boats in sheltered water.
That’s what makes the Inland waters different.
